title: Primary school teacher navigating phased return with Long COVID and POTS
transcript:
[00:00:08] INT: Right, so the recorder is running now. Thanks again for agreeing to take part in the Working with Long COVID study, Chloe. Just for the tape, I'm Dr. Samira Okafor from Pennine Valley University. Before we dive into the main questions, could you just tell me a little bit about yourself, your job, and your household?
[00:00:29] P: Yeah, of course. Um, so I'm Chloe Bramwell, I'm thirty-four—well, thirty-five next March, my birthday's the 12th of March 1989. I'm a primary school teacher at Brackenbridge Primary School, just here in Brackenbridge. I've been in the Year 2 team—well, Key Stage 1 team—for about eight years now. I live over in Low Moor, just on 14 Ashbourne Terrace, with my husband Gareth and our two kids. Theo's seven and Maisie's just turned four, so she's literally just started reception.
[00:01:05] INT: Oh, big milestone for Maisie! And how long have you been living with Long COVID now?
[00:01:12] P: Um, it's been... god, nearly a year. I first tested positive on the 14th of November 2022. I remember the exact date because it was the Monday after Remembrance Sunday and I was supposed to be doing a parents' evening. At first I just thought, right, it's a nasty dose, I'll be back in a week. I actually dragged myself back into school for the last two weeks of term in December because, you know, nativity plays and everything, you don't want to let the kids down. And then over Christmas I just completely crashed. I couldn't get off the sofa. I ended up being signed off properly on the 9th of January 2023.
[00:01:58] INT: That sounds really tough, trying to push through December like that. What were the symptoms like when you crashed?
[00:02:06] P: It wasn't just being tired, it was this crushing fatigue, like someone had poured concrete into my legs. And my heart—honestly, I thought I was having a heart attack at one point. I'd stand up to make a cup of tea and I'd get these awful heart palpitations and dizzy spells. Plus the shortness of breath. I've always had mild asthma, so I was hammering my Salbutamol inhaler, thinking it was that, but it wasn't touching it. And then the brain fog kicked in. That's the bit that really terrified me, to be honest. I'd be trying to read Theo a bedtime story and I couldn't process the sentences. I'd have word-finding difficulties just talking to Gareth in the kitchen—I'd be pointing at the kettle calling it 'the hot water box'.
[00:02:56] INT: How did your GP respond when you went to them with all of that?
[00:03:01] P: To be fair, my GP, Dr. Alistair Finch at Millgate Medical Practice, he's been brilliant. A bit overstretched, obviously, like they all are, but he actually listened. He ran all the bloods, ECGs, chest X-ray, and then in March he referred me to the Long COVID Clinic over at Cragside General Hospital in Tarnham. The wait was a nightmare, though. I remember ringing the booking line three times in one week, reciting my NHS number—999 482 7103, I've got it memorised off by heart now—just to check they hadn't lost the referral. When I finally got seen in May, they diagnosed me with Long COVID and also Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome, or POTS, which explained the racing heart.
[00:03:52] INT: Did they put you on any medication for the POTS or the other symptoms?
[00:03:57] P: Yeah, they tried me on Propranolol first, which made my asthma flare up a bit, so Dr. Finch switched me to Ivabradine. That's helped settle the heart rate a lot, actually. And I'm on Fexofenadine as well, an antihistamine, because the clinic said it sometimes helps with the inflammation and the post-exertional malaise. It's not a magic bullet, mind. If I overdo it on a Tuesday, I'm flat on my back by Thursday.
[00:04:28] INT: You mentioned post-exertional malaise—how does that affect your day-to-day life, and I suppose your sense of who you are?
[00:04:38] P: [sighs] Oh, it's completely stripped me of who I was. Before all this, I was the person who never sat still. At school, I'm not just a class teacher, I'm also the SENCO lead for deaf and hard-of-hearing pupils—I did my British Sign Language Level 3 qualification a few years back, which I loved. And outside of work, I used to do competitive bell-ringing—campanology—up at the parish church, and Gareth and I keep and breed Sebright bantams in the back garden. I haven't been up the bell tower in ten months. Even just going out to clean the chicken coop wipes me out for the rest of the afternoon. You grieve for your old self, you really do. You feel like a ghost in your own house.
[00:05:32] INT: That's a really powerful way of putting it. When it came to talking to your employer about all of this, what was that disclosure process like?
[00:05:42] P: Scary. Really scary. My headteacher is Patricia Hargreaves—Trish—and she's generally lovely, very supportive on a personal level, but she's under massive pressure from the governors and the local authority about budgets and cover. When I first told her in February that it was Long COVID and I didn't know when I'd be back, I could hear the panic in her voice. Not directed at me, just... how do you plan for an open-ended illness in a small school? I felt so guilty. I actually got in touch with my rep from the Northern Teachers' Union early on, just so I knew my rights, because I was terrified of going down the capability route.
[00:06:30] INT: Did you have an Occupational Health assessment before you started your phased return?
[00:06:35] P: Yes, through WellWork Solutions, who the council uses. I spoke to an advisor called Mark Tomlinson in July—I've still got the paperwork sitting on my desk here, reference OH-2023-8841. He was actually really good. He wrote a very clear report saying I needed a slow, twelve-week phased return, no playground duty, no after-school clubs, and a quiet space to sit down if my heart rate spiked. Trish agreed to all of it, to be fair to her. So I started back on the 4th of September 2023, just doing three mornings a week—Monday, Wednesday, Friday—so I've got a recovery day in between.
[00:07:20] INT: How has the phased return been going so far?
[00:07:25] P: Mixed, if I'm honest. The kids are gorgeous, and being back in the classroom reminded me why I love teaching. My teaching assistant, Denise Kowalski, has been an absolute saint. If she sees me losing my words or looking a bit grey, she just smoothly steps in and takes over the phonics group without making a fuss. She brings me water, reminds me to sit on the stool instead of standing at the whiteboard. Without Denise, I don't think I'd have lasted a fortnight. The hard part is the invisible stuff. Some of the other staff see me laughing in the staffroom on a Monday morning and assume I'm cured. They don't see me getting home at half-twelve and sleeping until four o'clock.
[00:08:15] INT: And what happens at the end of the twelve weeks? Have you got a review coming up?
[00:08:21] P: Yeah, my next review with Trish and Mark is on the 18th of October 2023. I'm dreading it, to be honest, because the expectation is that I'll be building back up to full-time by Christmas, and I just don't think my body can do it. Even three mornings is pushing me right to the edge. If I drop my hours permanently, we can't afford it.
[00:08:47] INT: Can you tell me a bit more about the financial side of things? How has being off sick affected you and Gareth?
[00:08:55] P: It's been brutal. On full-time I was earning £36,500 a year, which isn't a fortune, but with Gareth's wages we were comfortable. Under the teachers' sick pay scheme I got full pay for a hundred working days, and then in June I dropped to half pay, which works out at about £1,240 a month after tax. Before the phased return kicked in, we were looking at dropping down to Statutory Sick Pay—£109.40 a week—if I couldn't get back in September. Our mortgage alone is £950 a month! So that was a huge reason I pushed to go back when I did, probably before I was really ready. I did apply for Personal Independence Payment—PIP—back in May, just to try and bridge the gap, because even £280 a month would have helped with the bills, but they rejected it. Said because I can drive five minutes to the school, I don't qualify. I haven't got the energy to appeal it right now.
[00:10:02] INT: That sounds like an enormous amount of pressure to be carrying while you're trying to recover. How has all of that—the money, the fatigue—affected things at home with Gareth and the kids?
[00:10:15] P: [pauses, voice wavers] It's put a real strain on us, I won't lie. Gareth's been picking up every bit of overtime he can get, so he's exhausted too. And then he comes home and the house is a tip, tea isn't made, and I'm lying in bed with the curtains shut. He tries so hard to be patient, he really does, but sometimes you can just feel the resentment simmering under the surface. And the guilt with Theo and Maisie... [sniffs] Sorry. It just gets me. Theo's old enough to notice. Last week he asked me if I was 'broken forever'. That just shattered me. I can't kick a football around the garden with him anymore. I can't take Maisie swimming. You feel like you're failing at being a mum, failing at being a wife, and failing at being a teacher.
[00:11:16] INT: Take your time, Chloe, there's no rush at all. Do you want to pause for a minute?
[00:11:22] P: No, I'm okay, sorry. Just needed a tissue. It's actually a relief to say it out loud to someone who isn't going to try and 'fix' me or tell me to try yoga, you know?
[00:11:36] INT: Absolutely. And looking ahead, what do you feel you need most right now—from work, or from healthcare—to make staying in work sustainable?
[00:11:47] P: Flexibility, really. And just... belief. If Brackenbridge Primary could let me stay on three days—or even four mornings—without it feeling like I'm a burden, I think I could actually keep doing the job I love, especially the BSL and SENCO work, which I can do in smaller, quieter groups. And from the NHS side, just better join-up. Dr. Finch is great, and the Cragside General clinic is great, but they barely talk to each other, and neither of them talks to Occupational Health. You end up being the project manager of your own illness when your brain literally doesn't work.
[00:12:31] INT: That's a really important point, thank you. We're coming to the end of my questions now. Is there anything else you wanted to add that we haven't covered?
[00:12:41] P: No, I think I've talked your ear off enough! Just hope it helps other people who are stuck in this weird limbo.
[00:12:49] INT: It really will, thank you so much. Before I stop the recording, can I just double-check the best contact details for you so I can send over the £25 thank-you voucher and a summary of the study findings later in the year?
[00:13:02] P: Yeah, sure. My personal email is best—it's chloe.bramwell@example.org. And if you need to text me or anything, my mobile is 07700 900412.
[00:13:15] INT: Brilliant, I've got those down. I'll stop the recording now.

identifiers.text: SENCO lead for deaf and hard-of-hearing pupils
